A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same source-preference study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching results relocated between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on 13 LLMs, repetition-bias mitigation with GEMMA-3-4B, and additional validation and robustness results in its appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional abstention experiments, prompting comparisons and fine-tuning results averaged over seven training runs.

M1.justification: Section 6 substantively revises the reported consistency objective. In v1, the second KL term compares the teacher on repeated inputs with the student on unrepeated inputs; v3 compares unrepeated teacher predictions with repeated student predictions. The main-text loss weight also changes from 0.75 to 0.2. The teacher–student LoRA framework remains, but its stated training objective changes materially.

E1.justification: Section 4.4 adds conflict resolution with an explicit option to abstain, extending evaluation beyond v1's compulsory factual choice. The underlying English NeoQA data, seven entity types and source families remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v3 adds a repetition-aware prompting comparator that explicitly instructs models to disregard repetition. Credibility-only prompting remains evaluated: v1 Figures 10 and 29–31 correspond to v3 Figures 32–35. The 13-model roster remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The mitigation evaluation changes from holding out source instances/templates to withholding government and social-media source types entirely from training. Appendix J in v1 versus K in v3 changes the training/validation split from 1460/40 to 1275/225, batch size from 8 to 32, learning rate from 2e-4 to 1e-4, LoRA rank from 16 to 8, and final retention training from 300 to 200 steps. The new abstention experiment uses three numerical answer options and six table/answer arrangements.

E4.justification: New Section 4.4 directly tests whether source preferences are an artifact of compulsory answering. The revised mitigation experiment tests transfer to unseen source types, and repetition-aware prompting adds another mitigation analysis. Conversely, v1 Appendix J's fine-tuning-only ablation and Figure 32 are removed. Existing prompt-stability, position-bias and source-feature controls remain.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports fine-tuning averages and standard deviations across seven seeds, with training entities varying across runs, in Section 6 and Figure 11. v1 provides no equivalent repeated-run reporting for these results. The existing 10,000-resample bootstrap procedure, significance threshold and Holm–Bonferroni correction remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Section 6 replaces the reported maximum mitigation reduction of 99.8% in v1's abstract/results, inconsistently 95.9% in its introduction, with 79.2%; retained preference changes from 88.8% to 72.5%. Government/social-media mitigation changes from 86.9% to 78.3%. These are results under revised settings, not a same-setting performance decline. Section 4.4 and Table 1 add abstention outcomes, including retention of the original hierarchy for 11 of 13 models. Figure 8 also changes, and LLAMA-3.1-70B is no longer reported as an exception to repetition preference.

T1.justification: The Section 6 loss equation changes the mathematical definition of the repetition penalty by exchanging which contexts enter the teacher and student distributions. This is more than a notation change. The source-preference definitions remain equivalent, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central hierarchy, repetition vulnerability and mitigation contributions remain. v3 lowers the headline mitigation and preference-retention claims, explicitly claims mitigation generalization to source types absent from training, and extends the conclusion to preferences persisting when abstention is available.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the abstention experiment as evidence that source preferences extend beyond compulsory answering. It expands the rationale for synthetic sources as controlling biases associated with particular real sources and qualifies repetition-aware prompting as potentially unrealistic. The limitations remove the inability-to-abstain restriction and more explicitly identify unresolved generalization across knowledge conflicts, contexts and tasks.

D1.justification: Appendix J becomes Appendix K and substantially revises the fine-tuning recipe, including parameter counts, data partitioning and optimization settings. It removes the explicit loss-weight search grid and several intermediate data-construction counts. A material inconsistency is introduced: Section 6 states lambda = 0.2, whereas Appendix K states lambda = 200, leaving the intended implementation value unresolved. The code/data release information remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Six cited works are added: Yang and Menczer and Prama and Islam on prompted credibility assessment; Dai et al. and Khan et al. on source preferences; and Madhusudhan et al. and Tam et al. on abstention-related behavior. These refine the positioning in Sections 4 and 7 without replacing the existing related-work framework. The Gemma reference is relocated, not newly added.

P1.justification: v3 expands the introduction and credibility background, revises the conclusion and selected explanations, adds Section 4.4, and separates repetition-aware and credibility-only prompting into Appendices I and J. Terminology and references receive local edits. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains source-feature annotations and a mitigation-results panel; Table 1 adds abstention probabilities; and Figure 11 gains uncertainty bars. Prompting plots are added and reorganized across the main text and Appendices I/J, while v1's fine-tuning-only plot is removed. Most existing figures retain their design, and the two-column layout remains.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v1's compulsory-answering limitation and strengthens mitigation evidence through unseen-source-type evaluation and seven-run variability reporting. The revised loss equation also better matches the stated consistency objective. These gains improve support for the conclusions, but removal of the fine-tuning-only ablation and the new lambda = 0.2 versus 200 contradiction limit component attribution and reproducibility. The net improvement is therefore modest; lower headline results under changed settings do not establish a performance deterioration.
